#4547. Germany’s EV share hits record 37% as BEVs beat gas and diesel combined

Battery-electric cars took a record 37% of Germany’s new car market in October, according to data released today by the Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt (KBA), the country’s federal motor vehicle authority. That’s 94,086 BEVs, up 79.5% from 52,425 a year earlier.

For the second month in a row, German buyers registered more fully electric cars than gasoline and diesel cars combined. And with two months left in the year, Germany has already blown past the auto industry’s EV forecast for all of 2026.

The overall market barely grew in October. Total new car registrations rose 1.7% to 254,492 units, which means the EV growth came straight out of combustion cars.

Gasoline car registrations crashed 40.5% to 38,516 units, a 15.1% share. Diesel fell 21.6% to 23,882 units, or 9.4% of the market. Add them up and pure combustion cars made up just 24.5% of new registrations, 12.5 points less than BEVs alone.

Plug-in hybrids slipped 7.9% to 28,499 units (11.2%). So plug-ins accounted for about 48% of the German market last month, and the average CO2 emissions of new cars dropped 21.1% year-over-year to 79.4 g/km.

As we reported this summer, BEVs became the most popular powertrain in Germany for the first time in June with a 28.4% share. They’ve kept climbing every month since: 32.4% in August, 34.5% in September, and now 37% in October.

Through the first ten months of the year, Germany has registered 698,230 BEVs, up 60.7% year-over-year. That’s about 28.2% of the 2,476,290 new cars registered in 2026 so far, up from roughly 19% for the full year 2025.

And the industry didn’t see it coming. In December, the VDA, Germany’s auto industry association, forecast about 693,000 BEV registrations for all of 2026. Germany passed that in October. At the current pace, it’s on track for somewhere around 875,000 by the end of the year.

The biggest driver is Germany’s new EV incentive, which applies retroactively to cars registered since January 1. It pays €3,000 for a new BEV, bought or leased, and up to €6,000 for lower-income households with children. Households with taxable income above €80,000 (€90,000 with kids) don’t qualify.

The program targets private buyers, and that’s exactly where the KBA data shows the jump. Private registrations rose 20.6% in October, while commercial registrations fell 8.2%. Private buyers now make up 40.7% of the market.

Germany has been here before. The government killed its previous EV incentive overnight in December 2023, and BEV sales fell off a cliff in 2024. This time, the money is going to the buyers who need it most, and it’s moving the needle fast.

Tesla’s German numbers swing wildly with its quarterly delivery cycle. In September, the end of the quarter, it registered 12,552 cars (+268.7%) and the Model Y was the best-selling car in Germany. In October, it registered only 2,932, which is still up 290.9% but from a tiny base, for a 1.2% market share.

Year-to-date, Tesla is up 206.1% to 47,742 registrations. That’s a big rebound from a terrible 2025, but BYD is now slightly ahead with 47,961 (+216.1%). BYD registered 5,173 cars in October (+54.3%), though the majority of its German sales are plug-in hybrids, not BEVs.

The other Chinese brands are growing even faster. Leapmotor registered 3,661 cars in October, up 288.6%, and is at 19,705 for the year. Xpeng was up 284.4% to 1,380 units, and SAIC’s MG was up 48.5% to 4,140.

Volkswagen Group still owns the top of the EV charts, though. Through September, the Skoda Elroq was Germany’s best-selling EV with 30,845 units, ahead of the Tesla Model Y (29,464) and the VW ID.3 (24,352).

The EV boom is happening during one of the worst years in the history of Germany’s auto industry.

In October, the VW brand’s German registrations fell 4%, Audi dropped 8.4%, Porsche lost 5.7%, and Opel crashed 24.1%. BMW was flat (+0.1%), and Mercedes was the exception, up 8.5%. VW is still by far the biggest brand in Germany with an 18.2% share, but it’s down 5.6% for the year.

Last week, Volkswagen Group reported a €5.9 billion operating loss for the third quarter, its biggest quarterly loss since Dieselgate, driven by a writedown of its Porsche stake, weak sales in China, and thin EV margins. The group has already approved a plan to cut 100,000 jobs and close several German plants. Mercedes cut its 2026 car margin guidance to 2-3% last week, mainly because of China.

It’s not a product problem. VW’s new ID. Polo is sold out with over 30,000 orders, BMW has over 50,000 orders for the Neue Klasse iX3, and the Elroq leads the German EV market.

Germany is proving what we’ve been saying for years. Give buyers EVs they can actually afford, and they switch fast. Fully electric cars went from about 19% of the market last year to 37% in October, and the country beat the industry’s full-year forecast with two months to spare. That’s not a slow transition.

One thing to consider when talking about EVs not being Germany-made is that Germany car makers can't make them fast enough. A lot of the models are sold out for months. It's not an excuse but something to keep in mind.

Compare that with North America, where EV sales dropped 44% after the US killed its federal EV tax credit. Same technology, sometimes the same cars. The difference is policy.

Germany’s problem is who’s capturing the demand. Hint: it’s not German automakers.

But whose fault is that? You can’t spend years dragging your feet on electrification and lobby government back and forth on EV incentives and then complain when those who are all-in on EVs are able to take better advantage of the customer shift amid another oil crisis.

#4546. Range Rover is axing its two cheapest SUVs, making way for a new entry-level EV

Range Rover is pulling the plug on its two most affordable models, the Evoque and Velar, as a new entry-level EV steps in.

For decades, the Range Rover name was viewed as a status symbol, mostly used by wealthy buyers, high-powered executives, and even royalty.

That started to change with the launch of the Evoque in 2011 and the Velar in 2017, making the iconic British luxury brand a little more accessible.

In the US, the 2026 Range Rover Evoque starts at $49,900, and the Velar starts at $61,600. That’s considerably less than the Sport and flagship Range Rover SUVs, which start at $83,700 and $107,400, respectively.

Range Rover’s accessible luxury era is reportedly drawing to a close. Martin Limbert, Range Rover’s managing director, confirmed to Autocar that the Evoque and Velar will officially be discontinued, with production set to end in 2027.

While it has no direct replacement planned, the new Range Rover GT will serve as the brand’s new entry-level vehicle.

Range Rover revealed the GT in July, presenting it as the fifth and newest member of the lineup. Unlike the distinct SUV design Range Rover has built the brand on, the GT is a low-slung grand tourer.

The electric GT is “a captivating new expression” of the brand, Range said, describing it as “the most technologically sophisticated” model it’s ever designed.

It’s expected to be among the first vehicles based on JLR’s new EMA platform. Initially, the Range Rover GT will launch as a battery-electric vehicle (BEV), but Range Rover plans to add a full-hybrid (HEV) option later in the lifecycle.

Production of the Range Rover GT is set to begin in the first half of 2027 at JLR’s Halewood, UK plant, following the flagship electric SUV and smaller Sport EV model (shown below).

The Range Rover GT is expected to start at around $90,000 with an EPA range of at least 300 miles when it goes on sale as a 2028 model. In the UK, it will likely be over £75,000 ($100,000).

Range Rover’s flagship electric SUV starts at $140,450 in the US, and the smaller Sport EV will likely be a bit cheaper at around $120,000 to $130,000.

At $90,000, the electric GT isn’t what most would consider an “entry-level” vehicle, but it’s part of Range Rover’s push into higher-end, more profitable models.

#4541. Ford Fathom EV pickup prices will range from $28,350 to the high $30Ks

Ford’s upcoming Fathom electric pickup will be among the most affordable EVs in the US, starting at $28,350. Even pricier trims will start at under $40,000.

After announcing the name of its new midsize electric pickup this summer, Ford said the Fathom will start at just $28,350 for the standard-range model.

Even with the $1,595 delivery fee, prices will start at under $30,000. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week, CEO Jim Farley said the Fathom, Ford’s first vehicle off the Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform, remains on track to launch in Q4 2027.

Last Tuesday, a day before earnings, Farley said he had the chance to test-drive a prototype and that it “completely blew me away.”

The 0 to 60 mph, huge room inside, and the hands-free, ADAS experience was like “something I’ve never experienced,” Farley told investors.

Ford’s CEO added that the Fathom is a “breakthrough product” that’s highly capable and affordable. The MSRP under $30,000 and low cost of ownership, Farley said, is perfect for today’s market.

The electric pickup will use a zonal electrical architecture and a 48-volt system to cut costs. It will also offer bidirectional charging, enabling it to power your home to save on energy costs or during an outage.

When asked how the company plans to upsell the Fathom beyond the $28,350 starting price, Andrew Frick, president of Ford Model e, offered some insight.

“The starting price of $28,350 is just that,” Frick said. “We’ll have a range that goes to the high $30,000 range. And we’ll have a couple of different offerings within that,” he explained.

Frick said it’s too soon to share more about the offerings themselves at this point, and more details will come closer to launch.

According to Farley, the embedded Apple Maps is a “game changer” for any EV, but especially for a vehicle starting under $30,000.

“That is going to be the most exciting upsell opportunity,” Farley said, “it’s really the long-term subscription and digital experience for the customer.”

Apple Maps will be directly integrated into the navigation system. All Fathom models will be BlueCruise-capable for hands-free driving with standard Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

We still haven’t seen the interior, but Ford claims the Fathom has a “large touchscreen display” with easy-to-use navigation.

I almost feel like the Fathom will be utilized similarly to how the Maverick is utilized and possibly become a big seller as well. It seems well suited for a small business work vehicle as well with fuel savings by going electric to add to the appeal.

The midsize electric pickup will offer more interior space than a Toyota RAV4, and that’s not including the frunk (front trunk) or truck bed. Ford also said the Fathom will cost less to own over five years than a three-year-old used Tesla Model Y.

We also know the Fathom will have an NACS port after a prototype was caught at a Tesla Supercharger a few months ago.

Ford is set to open preorders in early 2027, with an official launch expected in the fourth quarter of 2027.

#4540. The 2027 Mercedes-AMG GT 63 4-Door Coupe Turns a New Page for AMG

An EV that sounds, and often feels, like it has been inspired by AMG’s V-8-powered past.

The 2027 Mercedes-AMG GT 63 4-Door Coupe marks an entirely new era for AMG. There isn’t a lick of hardware shared between this electric performance sedan and the milquetoast AMG EVs that came before it. The same goes for its drive software, which is as equally important as the exotic electric powertrain hiding under the car’s polarizing metal and LEDs. More than anything, this car is a statement to the world that Mercedes and AMG mean business in the cutthroat world of rapidly evolving electric performance.

It is familiar to AMG’s combustion offerings on purpose. Twist the dial over to Sport+ on the steering wheel, and the most convincing engine and transmission simulation in an EV yet comes to life. There’s no blend between electric motor and gasoline sounds to be heard here. It’s the twin-turbo 4.0-liter V-8 from the previous-generation AMG GT R Coupe, and it’s quite the circus act.

Mercedes calls it AMGFORCE Sport+ (a terrible name), and engineers took over 100 measurements with 16 microphone positions that allowed software gurus to reconstruct the sound digitally. What makes it convincing isn’t the sound, though. Mercedes uses the Burmester 4D sound exciters in the seats that produce vibrations with music to replicate the vibration and harshness you’d feel if a real V-8 were running up and down its rev range. You have to surrender your brain to the simulation, but if you do, it works. I was cackling in the driver’s seat all day, but you can just as easily turn off the fun and games for a pure EV soundscape.

Like other systems that do the same (see the Hyundai Ioniq 5 and the Genesis GV60), the AMG multiclutch transmission is fully simulated too. With a “redline” at 7200 rpm, the car lets you manually shift through seven speeds via steering-wheel-mounted paddles. Downshifts are accompanied with realistic engine braking on the overrun. Sadly, you can’t bang it off a simulated rev limiter at the top of each “gear,” but it’s still a hoot. If there’s a downside to this system, it’s the fake noise being piped to the outside world. Similar to Dodge’s cringey Fratzonic exhaust, Mercedes uses an exterior speaker system to project V-8 sounds from the rear of the car. Once the myth is busted, this is not convincing anybody and is likely to make a driver the butt of many a joke at the local Cars & Coffee.

V-8 clone technology aside, the AMG GT 63 4-Door Coupe produces numbers that should make even the staunchest of doubters raise an eyebrow in interest. Three axial flux motors—two in the rear and one in front—engineered with YASA combine to produce 1153 hp and 1475 lb-ft of torque. That peak power is accomplished in either Race or Boost mode, but don’t fret about it being temporary. Boost mode lasts a wild 63 seconds should you want it, and AMG says it could truly continue for as long as you desire in Race with zero derating. Standard, continuous output in other modes sits at 711 hp.

My first drive was at the gorgeous Ascari racetrack in southern Spain. It’s the ideal place to test out the car’s claimed 0–60-mph time of 2.3 seconds, and while I didn’t come close to the electronically limited 186-mph top speed, its rapid pull up to and beyond 130 mph suggests the limiter won’t take too long to reach.

There are several keys to this big sedan’s ability to run lap after lap at the track. One is direct oil cooling for the motors and gearsets, this using a proprietary, secret oil. Next, Mercedes uses water-cooled silicon carbide inverters. And finally, the most important piece is the 106-kWh, 800-volt AMG High Performance Electric Battery. This battery pack was developed specifically for AMG models (it won’t be used elsewhere) and uses unique cells with electrically nonconducting cooling oil flowing around each one.

The thermal management going on here is second to none, and on top of the track performance, it enables DC fast-charging at speeds beyond 600 kilowatts. That’s faster than any other EV on sale in America today. No, there aren’t any charging stations in the U.S. to support that madness, but Mercedes wheeled out a charger for a demonstration at Ascari, and I witnessed speeds of over 630 kilowatts. The claim is 10–80 percent in only 11 minutes, and given the right charger, this car can make that happen.

Lots of power doesn’t necessarily make a great EV, but that’s where AMG’s software wizards come into play. This tri-motor setup is truly only as competent as the software that’s running it, because there isn’t a single center differential or torque-vectoring diff to be found. Mercedes installed three completely independent electric motors with an absurd amount of torque and then went about making that controllable. Engineers tell me repeatedly that among the challenges, dialing in the proper drive characteristics was the biggest of all.

Funnily enough, this newfound flexibility in the powertrain led AMG to develop a set of dials with nine settings each it calls “AMG Race Engineer.” The Response Control dial lets you change throttle sensitivity, ranging from entirely dull to jumpy on the high end. A Traction Control dial does exactly what you’d expect, with one ensuring the car won’t slip an inch and nine turning the car into a full-on drift machine—there’s a Drift mode that shuts off the front motor too. Last, and most intriguing, there’s Agility Control. In practice, it’s like having an infinitely adjustable yaw controller at your beck and call. At one, it’s all understeer as you brake and steer into a corner. Dial it up to around the five-to-seven range, and the AMG transforms into a car with shockingly neutral balance, letting me induce just enough oversteer to coax the rear into a corner as I trail it in. Go all the way to nine, and you better watch yourself with how much the rear is going to be moving.

I’ve never driven a car that can behave so differently from corner to corner simply at the twist of a dial, but that’s the kind of freedom afforded by three extremely powerful, independent electric motors. When asked how the magic happens, engineers rattle on about how they’ve simulated differentials just by using positive and negative motor torque. Sometimes the car will be using brake regeneration at specific corners to induce the behavior you’ve selected; other times traditional brake torque vectoring intrudes to pinch the calipers to control the car’s movements. It all sounds like an impossible orchestra to compose, and yet somehow, they nailed it. All the way down to the adjustable traction control that lets you choose just how sideways you want to get accelerating out of a corner. Lock it down for safety, or send plumes of smoke into the air. The choice is genuinely entirely yours.

After a few laps of getting acclimated to how all these systems interact, I started to understand this big four-door’s personality. Around a racetrack, it drives similar to a Porsche Taycan that doesn’t take life so seriously. Or in other words, it drives how you’d expect an AMG product to, safely sliding around and roaring its V-8 trumpet.

The 63 comes with AMG’s Ride Control air suspension with active roll stabilization that uses the same hydraulically interconnected dampers as you’d find on the AMG GT 63 Coupe, allowing chassis engineers to delete the anti-roll bars. I didn’t drive the 63 on the road, but the ride over curbing was considerably better than I expected from a 5534-pound performance sedan that corners as flat as it does. Active aero in the form of underbody Venturi flow elements, a deployable rear spoiler, an extendable rear diffuser, and front cooling louvers keep the car in either the most advantageous aerodynamic profile for range or in maximum-downforce-and-stability mode.

The brakes are mighty, with carbon-ceramic rotors up front and steel rotors in the rear. Huge recuperation capability from the axial-flux electric motors means they don’t even have to work very hard. Despite eight laps around Ascari, there was hardly a whiff of brake smell when I pulled back into pit lane—yet another shock for a large and heavy EV. Unfortunately, brake feel is a sore point, with the pedal offering an airy sensation through the first half before firming up toward the bottom of the stroke. Braking distances seem comparable to other large performance sedans in practice, in part due to the Michelin Pilot Sport S 5 tires Mercedes fits. More aggressive Cup 2 tires would take this car to another level, but it’s a step engineers were hesitant to take with this model, perhaps saving the grippier rubber for a more extreme version to come.

My other biggest gripe: The fake V-8 and transmission disappear in Race mode. Outside of Sport+, this EV accelerates and sounds like any other megaquick electric car. It’s unending, brutal, and, eventually, a bit boring. Thankfully, the slidetastic chassis keeps things entertaining on the racetrack, though I suspect the number of owners who bring this beast to the track will be in the double digits at best. You can technically bring it there and pound around with none of the typical downsides of pushing an EV, but this AMG is no track star.

The AMG GT 63 4-Door Coupe starts at $176,500, which sure sounds high, but at the same time reasonable with how much effort AMG put into this car from a hardware, software, and material perspective. It’s also right in line with a Porsche Taycan Turbo, the GT 63’s closest competitor.

If you’re inclined to such an experience in an EV, there’s no better internal-combustion simulator in existence. Combine this party trick with the infinitely adjustable handling attitude, and you’re left looking at a technological fortress of performance. It’s one hell of a statement. I’m just not sure many people are going to be willing to listen to it.

#4539. GM is recalling more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs over a brake software defect

General Motors (GM) issued a recall affecting more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs because a software glitch can cause a temporary loss of braking.

The recall comes after a 2024 Cadillac Lyriq ran into a garage (at a low speed). On April 10, 2026, a GM tech expert submitted a report to GM’s Speak Up for Safety (SUFS) program for review.

After internal testing, GM was able to replicate the glitch, similar to a recall it issued in 2024. GM said the issue stems from a software glitch with the brake system control module (BSCM) that can cause a temporary loss of braking while driving under certain conditions.

When drivers lightly tap the brakes during a sharp turn and the vehicle hits a bump, the software’s slip calculation may misinterpret wheel movement.

In some instances, it can lead to a temporary loss of braking. The glitch only affects pAWD vehicles, including certain Cadillac Lyriq, Celestiq, Vistiq, and Chevy Blazer EV.

In a letter sent to the NHTSA on October 29, GM said the recall impacted 67,380 vehicles total, including certain:

According to documents filed with the NHTSA, GM found 24 field complaints related to the issue. Of these, 20 involved minor accidents, and two involved allegations of minor injuries.

The complaints were received between February 24, 2024, and June 11, 2026. GM said it has implemented software corrections in production over the past few months.

GM will update the BSCM software via an over-the-air (OTA) update or through a dealer, free of charge.

Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed out on December 14, 2026. In the meantime, you can contact Cadillac’s customer service at 1-800-333-4223 or Chevrolet’s customer service at 1-800-222-1020. GM’s recall number is N262570900.

You can also contact the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration Hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit the nhtsa.gov website for more information. The NHTSA campaign number is 26V717.

#4538. Florida Man Who Allegedly Stole $210,000 Porsche Panamera Apparently Forgot He Was Wearing a GPS Ankle Monitor

A previous police chase had earned the 19-year-old suspect a tracking device, which investigators say placed him at the scene of the Porsche theft.

We at Road & Track certainly don't know if a handbook for car thieves exists. But if it did, there would certainly have to be a chapter on how to avoid getting caught. And that chapter probably begins with some fairly obvious advice—like, for example, don't steal a $210,000 Porsche Panamera while wearing a GPS ankle monitor that tells the authorities exactly where you are.

According to a report by WPLG Local 10 News, 19-year-old Joseph Dexter Watson IV has been accused by authorities of participating in the October 24 theft of a Porsche Panamera. The luxury car was reportedly stolen from a multimillion-dollar mansion in Miami-Dade County's Horse Country neighborhood.

According to investigators, Watson and at least three accomplices arrived at the property in a Mercedes-Benz shortly before 6:30 p.m. The group allegedly broke into a Cadillac Escalade parked outside the gated property, but apparently not satisfied with the score, one of the suspects reportedly climbed over a fence and stole the Porsche. Inside the Panamera, authorities say, were seven pairs of shoes valued at roughly $4200. The Porsche's owner quickly tracked the car to a Hampton Inn parking lot in Deerfield Beach; When Broward Sheriff's Office deputies arrived, they found the Porsche, but nobody was inside.

However, locating one of the suspects was surprisingly easy. See, in January, Watson allegedly led police on a bizarre chase: according to authorities, the rented Kia he was driving crashed into a mail truck, when he then reportedly tried to hide in another mail truck before attempting to flee the scene in an Uber. Watson was caught and spent approximately two months in jail before being released on bond in March.

As a condition of his release, Watson was ordered to wear a GPS ankle monitor. According to investigators, it was that very monitor that placed him at the scene of the Porsche theft. He now faces new charges, including traveling with intent to commit burglary of an occupied dwelling, masked burglary of an occupied dwelling, and grand theft of a motor vehicle. He is being held at the Turner Guilford Knight Correctional Center—this time, without bond.

#4537. Driven: The Mercedes-AMG GT 4-Door Won’t Make You Wait

The Mercedes-AMG GT55 and GT63 EVs bring Formula 1 battery technology to the road.

The most shocking thing about the new Mercedes-AMG GT63 4-Door Coupe isn’t its 1475 pound-feet of torque or its 1153 horsepower. Or the estimated 2.0-second run to 60 mph. Or the flat cornering. Or the responsive steering. Or the drive modes that let you change how the GT doles out its three-motor grunt. It isn’t even the polarizing style. It’s that this car charges at at a rate of up to 600 kilowatts.

That kind of power makes replenishing the battery almost as quick as pumping gas. Mercedes says its new GT will go from 10 to 80 percent in just 11 minutes. In a demonstration we witnessed, the car was still pulling 259 kilowatts at 78 percent state of charge. Impressive stuff.

Of course, finding a 600-kW charger in the U.S. is another story. In Europe, these kinds of high-high-power DC chargers are increasing in popularity thanks to a growing quantity of heavy electric trucks. But even if you can’t find a charger that can provide more than 350 kW of juice, the GT63—and its less powerful sibling, the 805-hp GT55—can max that charger out for much longer than an EV with a 350-kW peak. As you might expect, both GT variants will come to the U.S. with NACS plugs.

See all results for new 2027 Mercedes-AMG GT 4-Door EV for sale near 60629

The 2027 GT 4-Door can do this thanks to a thermal strategy borrowed from Formula 1. The car’s 106-kWh battery pack, which consists of 2660 cells arranged in 18 modules, is oil cooled. The terminals of the individual cells are where the heat really builds during charging, and by using a cooling loop that focuses on those terminals first, engineers can pump more power into the battery without damaging the cells. This method keeps temps stable across the entire battery within a range of about 9 degrees.

EPA ranges are still TBD, but we expect both the GT55 and GT63 to break 300 miles in maximum-range configuration. Wheels and tires will play a role as they always do, but we mention a max-range config because the GT 4-Door packs a couple of optional active aerodynamic elements to boost range. A hidden front panel works in concert with an extendable rear diffuser, because extending the body’s total length reduces drag. (It’s also really interesting when the diffuser extends several inches beyond the rear bumper.) There are also some moving elements under the body work that increase downforce, but those are more for corner carving than for hypermiling. And, of course, the wing out back can adjust to reduce drag or increase downforce, depending on driving behavior.

The higher-zoot GT63 also comes packed with all manner of newfangled suspension hardware. Hydraulic anti-roll control and air springs support multilink geometries front and rear. All the suspension components are aluminum, except for the two rear upper links, which are stamped steel. The lower-power 55 gets conventional anti-roll bars instead of the hydraulic ones. Rear-axle steer, which can turn the rear rollers up to 6 degrees in either direction, is standard.

See all results for new 2027 Mercedes-AMG GT 4-Door EV for sale near 60629

Another clever addition is the use of aramid in the crash structure, a synthetic fiber you might recognize from its use in bulletproof vests. AMG lashes aramid rope (roughly the diameter of a hearty man’s pinkie finger) to the longitudinal chassis rails. In the event that the car hits a pole or a tree, the rope transfers the load to the chassis, and those longitudinal members crumple inward a bit, hopefully preventing the impact from involving the undoubtedly expensive front motor.

“Structural frunk” is a phrase we’re still getting used to saying out loud. The AMG GT 4-Door has a small frunk, yes, but it’s best used to store a charging cable or other small knickknacks you want to keep handy. Unlike your typical plastic frunk, though, this one is made of carbon fiber. The box bolts directly to the chassis, and it’s stiff enough that it boosts the torsional rigidity of the front end by 35 percent. It is also curved to direct airflow under the hood, so it has three purposes. (Serving as an ersatz beverage cooler does not count as a fourth.)

The AMG Dynamic Package, which is standard on the GT63 and optional on the GT55, brings three control knobs labeled Response, Agility, and Traction to the center console. These knobs, called Race Engineer, have a profound effect on the car’s behavior. The Response knob, available in all drive modes, plays with the accelerator calibration. Position one is a very lazy “throttle”; acceleration ramps up almost comically slowly. On the other side, position nine is a light switch. The Agility knob, which is only active in Sport, Sport+, and Race modes with stability control turned off, works in concert with what remains of the stability control, the front-to-rear torque split, and the rear-axle torque vectoring. Position one maintains a tight line, while nine allows for lurid drifts. The Traction knob, also only active in Sport, Sport+, and Race modes with stability control turned off, is pretty self-explanatory; nine almost eliminates the traction assist entirely.

Tinkering with these three knobs generates vastly different results. If you want to work on your driving line around a track, keep the Agility and Response knobs in positions one through three. The car keeps the body tight and perfectly meters power on corner exit. Crank them to seven or higher, and you’ll meet your new best friend: oversteer. Just mash the throttle and keep the front tires pointed where you want to go, and Race Engineer will handle the rest.

Sport+ is the only mode where fake powertrain sounds are pumped into the cabin. In addition to that synthetic soundtrack, a tachometer appears on the instrument screen, and the steering-wheel paddles change jobs from adjusting brake-regen levels to working virtual gears. The V-8 rumble, which includes shakers in the front seats, is based on the last-gen AMG GT R and manages a solid impersonation. Shifts arrive with an abrupt but brief interruption in torque; sure, the feeling is probably more pronounced than what’s felt from the actual GT R’s dual-clutch, but the theatrics are executed perfectly.

With the Agility and Response knobs set to seven, the GT63 drives much smaller than its 119.7-inch wheelbase and 5500-pound curb weight imply. Turn-in is crisp, and adroit steering corrections result in quick responses. You can even trail-brake this big car deep into corners while the Race Engineer algorithms help with rotation.

Driving around town, the GT55 is limited to 557 horses and the GT63 to 711, but a quick hop over to Race mode will call up all the remaining horses. Should you desire short periods of naughty driving, a boost mode achieves the same full-power blast, albeit in 55- and 63-second bursts (you can guess which model gets which duration). It’s not like you need four figures’ worth of horsepower to make a pass on a mountain road, but passengers will surely love it. Both variants are quiet and smooth riding, though not quite as smooth as an Active Ride–equipped Porsche Taycan.

Figuring out where the AMG lands among other high-power EV sedans will have to wait for a comparison test, but our first sampling indicates that the Merc splits the difference between the more spacious Lucid Air and the smaller Taycan. The GT’s interior is top-spec Mercedes, full of great materials and clever ergonomic touches. There’s a fair amount of customization through the central display, our favorite of which is the ability to rearrange and even hide some of the functions on the steering wheel knobs. Residents of Phoenix, for example, can remove Slippery mode from the mode-switching dial. Degenerates can set the dial to only include Comfort and Race. The sky’s the limit.

The 2027 Mercedes-AMG GT55 goes on sale later this year with a starting price of $146,550, undercutting the driver-focused Taycan GTS. When the 63 hits dealers next year for $176,550, it’ll likewise undercut on the Porsche Taycan Turbo. With this level of performance on board—both the charging and the hard-charging kind—the GT 4-Door should be quite a strong competitor.

#4536. First: Volvo CE Electric equipment does the work, without disturbing the wildlife

For the first time, electric equipment assets are being put to work in the National Wildlife Refuge System, where a battery-powered, zero-emission ECR25 Electric compact excavator and L25 Electric compact wheel loader made by Volvo CE are making the wild more accessible to everyone.

Construction work isn’t exactly welcome in the wilderness – between diesel exhaust, engine noises, and the constant rumble of heavy machinery, even a relatively small project can have a big impact on the native wildlife. To minimize that impact, US Fish and Wildlife Service is turning to Volvo CE and its compact excavators and wheel loaders to get the job done, building out a new, ADA accessible trail in Virginia’s Occoquan Bay National Wildlife Refuge.

“We are excited to partner with the US Fish and Wildlife Service on this project to demonstrate Volvo’s commitment to lowering emissions and working to build the future we all want and need,” said Dr. Ray Gallant, VP of Product Management and Productivity, Volvo CE. “Projects like the one at the Occoquan Bay National Wildlife Refuge give a glimpse of how electric machines can create a more climate-friendly future for the construction industry.”

The refuge is home to a diverse array of grasslands, wetlands, and woods that attract red foxes, painted turtles, osprey, river otters, and countless other rarely seen species – and the ADA accessible path being laid down by the L25 Electric compact wheel loader will allow wheelchair-bound visitors to travel a half-mile-long trail around one of the pond. Meanwhile, the ECR25 Electric compact excavator will be digging trenches to improve drainage from the pond and helping to place a viewing platform that extends out over the water.

Keeping the machines running is a portable EV ARC solar-powered charging system from Beam Global that’s designed to drive down the project’s carbon footprint even further.

#4535. High gas prices are pumping up used EV sales: these are FLYING off the lot

A new car affordability crisis and punishing gas prices are driving an unprecedented number of used car buyers to consider going electric, and that increased demand without a corresponding increase in supply means these used EVs are flying off dealer lots.

Days on the lot. That’s dealer-speak for the average number of days a given vehicle typically sits in inventory before finding a buyer. That’s critically important to dealers, since the vehicles on their lots are commonly financed through something called floorplan credit, and every additional day a car spends on a dealer’s lot can mean another day of interest payments and another day closer to a curtailment. Days on the lot can be even more important to dealers when it comes to cars owned outright, as well, as the dealers can have significant cash tied up in vehicles they’ve purchased outright, and every day those cars sit is another day that money isn’t working for them elsewhere.

That’s what makes this month’s fastest-selling used EVs particularly interesting, because these used EVs aren’t just selling fast for electric vehicles – they’re selling fast, period.

Dealer news sources Automotive News and Cox Automotive report that the average new car spent 82 days on the lot in October, with a 75-day target being an industry-wide benchmark. At the same time, the Audi Q4 Sportback e-tron Quattro with its 258-mile EPA-estimated range is turning in just 29.8 days. (!)

That Audi’s not alone. In a recently-released vehicle pricing study, iSeeCars reported that the Toyota BZ4x, Lexus RZ300e, Honda Prologue, and Borrás-family favorite Polestar 2 are all turning in an average of 35 days or less, with the BMW i4, iX, Kia EV6, and Chevrolet Equinox EV just a day or two behind.

“The results reveal a market where EVs are appreciating in average asking price much faster than other drivetrains, while also spending less time waiting for buyers,” said iSeeCars Executive Analyst Karl Brauer, who found that average transaction prices for EVs rose 9.8% last month as ICE-powered vehicles stayed steady, rising just 0.3%. “Hybrids are experiencing moderate improvements in price and selling speed, while gasoline-powered vehicles have seen their selling times increase,” he adds, “despite relatively stable prices.”

@Jo Borras , you forgot to mention about one more factor (besides: "A new car affordability crisis and punishing gas prices..."). Back in September last year there was still electric vehicle tax credits in the United States that has ended on September 30, 2025.

Used electric vehicles averaged a price of $32,533 in September 2026, up $2,896 from the $29,637 ATP recorded a year earlier.

#4534. The Toyota Supra and BMW Z4 Are Officially Sold Out: Report

Production for the sibling sports car pair has ended, and the last units in the U.S. have, apparently, left dealer lots.

When BMW and Toyota first joined forces to reimagine two iconic sports car nameplates—the Supra and the Z4—the collaboration was a surprise, but also turned out to be quite a success, at least in terms of the smiles both cars delivered. Six years later, Toyota and BMW are sunsetting production of the sibling sports cars, and shoppers have apparently bought out all the remaining inventory.

National inventory data analyzed by CarsDirect brought to broader attention by Motor1 indicates that all new Toyota GR Supra and BMW Z4 units have been sold. (Road & Track found a handful of new Supra and Z4 listings on Autotrader, for what it’s worth, but that info is subject to dealers remembering to update their listings.) Both manufacturers ended production of the sports cars, which were built at the Magna Steyr factory in Austria, back in March.

Despite genuine enthusiast love, neither the GR Supra nor the Z4 sold particularly well. Toyota sold 2953 GR Supras in 2025, while BMW sold 2113 units of the Z4. All told, around 31,228 GR Supra units were sold in the U.S. since 2020. Similarly, BMW sold about 15,282 units of the fifth-generation Z4 in the U.S.

BMW offered a Z4 Final Edition in December 2025 with Individual Frozen Black Metallic paint and a Moonlight Black soft top. Toyota also offered a Final Edition GR Supra in May 2026, featuring larger brakes, adjusted suspension, and matte black paint. 1300 Final Edition GR Supra units made it to the U.S.

Toyota has not officially announced plans for a sixth-generation GR Supra, though company executives said the sports car will likely return. “It would be logical that we would have a next-gen Supra. But when and how is still TBD,” senior vice president of Product Planning and Strategy for Toyota Motor North America Cooper Ericksen said to MotorTrend.

BMW, however, has no current plans to bring a sixth-generation roadster to production. It remains unclear if BMW will bring another roadster to market.

The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

#4533. BLUETTI’s flexible $1,099 Apex 200 backs up your home – and powers your RV

What do you actually need to keep running when the power goes out? For most households, the fridge, wifi, phones, and a few other essentials come first. Buying enough battery storage for every appliance in the house can come later – and that’s the appeal of BLUETTI’s latest launch, the Apex 200 portable power station.

The Apex 200 starts with 2.56kWh of storage and 3.2kW of continuous AC output, with the option to add batteries when you need longer backup. Built-in RV connections also mean it can earn its keep between blackouts.

BLUETTI launches the Apex 200 on November 4, with standalone super early-bird pricing starting at $1,099 through November 18. Electrek readers can get an extra 5% off with code ELECTREK5OFF.

Here’s how to work out which setup is worth buying for your home or RV.

The Apex 200 takes the expandable design of BLUETTI’s flagship Apex series and puts it in a smaller package.

You get a 2,560Wh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery. The 3.2kW of continuous AC output increases to 3.6kW when an expansion battery is connected or the unit is actively charging.

The enclosure holds all that in 36.2 liters and weighs 26.9kg (59.3 lb). You’ll want two hands to move it, but it’s convenient to move it between home and your camper.

BLUETTI’s UltraCell technology delivers an industry-leading energy density of 70.7 Wh/L, yet the Apex 200 is more than 50% smaller by volume than class competitors. For an RV owner, that smaller footprint frees up room for other gear.

There’s also a tilted display and four app-controllable AC outlets. That might not sound like a big deal, but when the battery is on the floor or under your desk and you want to check or redirect its charge, it means you don’t have to crouch.

BLUETTI calls its approach “Start Small. Scale Big. Power More.” BLUETTI says Apex 300 users reported liking the modular design but wanted something easier to handle day to day. The Apex 200 offers them a lower entry point, with room to add capacity rather than replace the main unit.

Before buying a portable power station, you’ll want to know how much power your appliances draw and how much energy they use over time.

For example, a 150W appliance running continuously for 10 hours uses 1,500Wh. A 1,500W appliance gets through that same amount in one hour. Running a coffee maker briefly is a different proposition from keeping a high-draw appliance on all afternoon.

A rough runtime calculation is: Usable battery capacity in watt-hours ÷ average load in watts = hours of operation.

Divide the Apex 200’s nominal 2,560Wh by a steady 150W load, and you get about 17 hours before accounting for conversion losses and the battery system’s own power use. Real runtime will be lower.

Refrigerators complicate that calculation because their compressors cycle on and off. Check measured daily energy use where possible, along with startup demand – motors can briefly draw more power when they kick on.

If your usual blackout lasts four to 12 hours, start by looking at the Apex 200 on its own.

BLUETTI estimates it can run a 150W refrigerator for 10–12 hours, or support low-draw essentials such as CPAPs, wifi routers, and mobile devices for two to three days, depending on the equipment and how it’s used. That doesn’t mean every device on that list will run together for three days. Your combined load determines the runtime.

The Apex 200 also gives you more control over where that energy goes. Four independently controllable Smart AC outlets built right into the unit – no need to buy smart plugs! – let you switch individual devices on and off through the BLUETTI App, set schedules, and apply state-of-charge controls. So if something doesn’t need power overnight, you can turn off its power at the outlet and save the fridge’s battery.

BLUETTI calls the feature an industry first for portable power stations. The system also works with Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and Home Assistant.

A UPS function switches connected equipment to battery power in 15 milliseconds. Check that switching time against your equipment’s requirements, especially for a CPAP or other sensitive device.

With AC output on and the display off, idle consumption drops to just 10.5W.

A winter freeze or severe storm can leave you without grid power for days. That’s when adding extra storage starts to make more sense.

For typical power outages, adding one or two BLUETTI B300K batteries can extend essential home backup to two to three days.

But you can go further. One Apex 200 supports up to six B500K expansion batteries, bringing its maximum capacity to 33.28kWh.

But a bigger battery still needs recharging eventually. The Apex 200 accepts up to 3kW of solar input across two independent channels:

With a correctly configured array of SORA 500 portable solar panels making full use of those inputs, BLUETTI says the base battery can charge from 0 to 80% in 50 minutes, or reach 100% in 1.7 hours using solar alone.

A solar generator setup lets you recharge during daylight. The Apex 200 can also be charged with wall AC, vehicle charging, and compatible gas-generator charging. A suitable 30A generator connection can help replenish the battery when solar production falls short.

The Apex 200 can also form part of a larger home battery backup system through BLUETTI’s Hub A1 parallel box.

BLUETTI specifies up to 6kW of continuous AC output and approximately 100kWh of storage across a parallel system using up to three Apex 200 units.

That’s a significant increase over the standalone battery, but your daily consumption still matters. A steady 1kW load uses 24kWh in 24 hours. Heavy-draw appliances can make a large battery feel much smaller.

BLUETTI positions its larger configurations for three to four days of essential-panel backup. How close you get depends on your batteries, appliances, and ability to recharge.

If you want automatic backup through your home’s electrical panel, confirm the compatible transfer equipment, supported circuits, voltage, and output for the exact bundle. Those details determine what you can actually keep running.

Start with your most likely outage, then decide whether you need more runtime, a charging source, or both.

Extra batteries extend runtime. Solar panels or another charging source recharge them. For outages that stretch into days, both can be worth having.

When shopping for a camper van or travel trailer, choosing a battery comes down to more than just capacity. Among its 10 output ports are two connections RV owners will appreciate having built in.

The native 30A TT-30R RV outlet plugs directly into travel trailer shore power inlets for 120V power.

The 12V/30A Anderson port can directly power compatible DC equipment, including portable fridges and communications gear. This avoids converting battery power to AC and then back to DC, cutting out unnecessary conversion steps.

For charging between campsites, the system can pair with the BLUETTI Charger 2, which combines alternator and solar charging support. It lets you use driving time to replenish the battery through faster vehicle alternator charging, then use solar when you’re parked.

BLUETTI’s recommended mobile bundle is the Apex 200 + SORA 500 solar panel + Charger 2. You get storage for camp, solar charging during your stay, and alternator charging on the road. Compatible campground AC gives you another option.

The Apex 200 is the better fit if you value a smaller enclosure, easier transport, native RV ports, and a lower upfront cost. You can start with 2.56kWh and expand to 33.28kWh on one unit, or approximately 100kWh across a fully expanded parallel system.

The Apex 300 is worth considering if your priority is higher native output and capacity for a system that will mostly stay at home. It offers 3,840W of output and 2,764.8Wh of battery storage, and BLUETTI positions it for more advanced home backup, including compatible 120V/240V configurations.

For someone who wants a battery for both blackouts and RV trips, the Apex 200’s size and connections make a useful combination. You can buy the storage you need now and add more when your power needs change.

The Apex 200 launches November 4, with the standalone unit starting at $1,099 during the November 4–18 super early-bird promotion.

Founded in 2013, BLUETTI allows millions of users across more than 120 countries to stay safe and prepared. Its in-house R&D supports a range of solar generators and home backup systems for outage preparation, RV travel, and off-grid living and recreation.

Shop the Apex 200 and launch bundles, and use ELECTREK5OFF at checkout for an extra 5% savings.

#4531. Aniioki A9 Pro Max review: Basically an electric motorcycle that you can pedal

There are electric bikes, there are electric motorcycles, and then there are machines like the Aniioki A9 Pro Max that plant a flag somewhere in the increasingly large no-man’s-land between the two.

Technically, it has pedals. You can pedal it fairly effectively too, with the actually adjustable seat. You can even pedal it for fun, which is more than I can say for some of the increasingly motorcycle-shaped “e-bikes” I’ve tested lately.

But let’s get something out of the way right at the beginning: this isn’t a street-legal electric bicycle in the US. Not when we’re talking about dual motors producing up to 6,000W of peak power and speeds of around 45 mph.

And you know what? That’s fine. As long as we’re all honest about what this thing is.

The Aniioki A9 Pro Max is absolutely massive, and the spec sheet makes that abundantly clear.

The version I tested uses a pair of 2,500W direct-drive hub motors, one in each wheel, with Aniioki claiming 3,000W peak power from each motor. That gives the bike a combined peak figure of 6,000W and up to 250 Nm of combined torque. It’s hard to overstate how massive that is.

Then there’s the battery. You can choose between a 60V 70Ah pack with 4.2 kWh of capacity or an even larger 60V 80Ah pack packing 4.8 kWh. For comparison, many typical commuter e-bikes have somewhere around 500-700 Wh of battery. The smaller battery here is roughly six to eight times that size. That’s absolutely in the territory of legit light electric motorcycles.

Aniioki claims up to 230+ miles (370 km) of pedal-assist range, though as usual, you should take maximum e-bike range figures as best-case numbers. Using the throttle and enjoying those big motors is going to dramatically reduce that figure. Even so, with more than 4 kWh of battery underneath you, range anxiety isn’t exactly the first thing that comes to mind.

All that hardware comes with a predictable penalty: weight. The 70Ah model tips the scales at around 188 lb (85 kg), while the 80Ah version approaches 193 lb (87.5 kg). Those aren’t e-bike weights. Those are motorcycle weights. Again, you can see the direction this is going.

Here’s where the A9 Pro Max gets more interesting to me.

A lot of high-powered e-motos include pedals seemingly as a regulatory fig leaf. They’re technically there, but the geometry is so bad that nobody in their right mind would want to pedal the thing farther than across a parking lot. Even some smaller and presumably Class 2 legal e-bikes that have moto-style frames are nearly unpedalable for actual riding over any reasonable distance.

But the A9 here is actually pedalable thanks to having something that more closely resembles a bicycle seat, plus adjustability that lets riders dial in the correct seat height.

The A9 Pro Max feels more like a strange combination of an oversized fat-tire e-bike and a small electric motorcycle. There’s a Shimano 7-speed drivetrain and a huge 72-tooth chainring, meaning the pedals aren’t entirely ornamental.

I actually enjoyed pedaling it with the pedal assist engaged. You’re obviously not going to mistake a nearly 200-pound machine rolling on enormous 26 x 4.8-inch tires for a lightweight fitness bike, but there’s something fun about contributing some human power while two giant hub motors do most of the heavy lifting.

And when you don’t feel like pedaling, there’s a full-twist throttle waiting for you.

That combination is really the appeal here. You can ride it more like an e-bike when the mood strikes, or twist the throttle and treat it more like a lightweight e-moto.

And again, I don’t want to beat a dead horse here, but remember: the pedals don’t make this an electric bicycle. It’s still an e-moto, but it’s one that you can actually have fun pedaling. You can treat it like a mech suit, where pedaling translates into crazy power, as if you have super-human legs. And with the insanely large 72t chainring, pedaling at higher speeds is actually doable. Though I’ll tell you right now, pedaling at 40 mph (64 km/h) is not exactly a normal or natural feeling.

And it’s worth pointing out that at a starting price of US $2,899 (or more for the larger battery capacities), that’s a fairly reasonable price compared to most e-motos that can be more limiting in how and where you can ride them.

Fortunately, Aniioki seems to understand that putting this much power on two wheels requires more serious components than the average bicycle.

The braking setup is particularly wild. There are two massive 300mm brake rotors on the front wheel and another 300mm rotor out back, along with a linked CBS braking system. The front uses custom eight-piston calipers (the pair of quad-piston calipers) while the rear gets a custom six-piston setup.

There’s also an adjustable air-suspension fork with 110mm of travel, rear suspension to smooth out bumps at higher speeds, integrated lighting and turn signals, and a large five-inch display that even incorporates features like Bluetooth audio and a recording camera.

That brings us to the elephant in the room.

In the US, consumer-product rules generally define a low-speed electric bicycle around a motor of less than 750W and a maximum motor-powered speed below 20 mph (32 km/h), while individual states use their own operating laws that typically match the familiar Class 1/2/3 framework. A 6,000W machine capable of around 45 mph (72 km/h) blows straight through normal limits.

So please don’t see pedals and assume this belongs on your local bicycle path.

Where and how you can legally operate something like the A9 Pro Max depends on your local laws and whether it can qualify under another vehicle category. For many owners, the sensible place to enjoy its full performance is going to be private property or other areas where such vehicles are permitted.

That caveat doesn’t make the bike itself bad. It just means buyers need to understand what they’re buying.

And judged on what it actually is rather than what the word “e-bike” on the product page suggests, I had a lot of fun on it.

There are certainly riders who would look at a nearly 200-pound, 45 mph machine and say, “Why not just buy an electric motorcycle?” That’s a perfectly reasonable question.

In addition to kW power limits, the legal boundary for what is an e-bike should also include weight. Anything over 100lbs including battery is no longer an e-bike and it carries a dangerous amount of momentum once it is cruising. 190 lbs is ridiculous.

But I also understand the appeal of this weird middle ground. The A9 Pro Max retains enough bicycle DNA that you can pedal it around and enjoy pedal assist, yet has enough battery and motor underneath you to deliver something much closer to small-motorcycle performance when you twist the throttle.

Imagine going off-road and getting to fly up hills while pedaling hard, but then being able to switch to throttle once your legs get worn out. Sure, it’s not everyone’s cup of tea, but it’s a cup of tea.

This bike is big. It’s heavy. It’s absurdly powerful by e-bike standards. And it absolutely isn’t the machine I’d recommend for someone looking for a normal street-legal electric bicycle.

But if what you actually want is a big, powerful electric two-wheeler that still lets you turn the pedals when the mood strikes, the Aniioki A9 Pro Max makes a surprisingly compelling argument for this increasingly bizarre category of pedal-equipped e-motos.

#4530. C8 Corvette Manual Conversion: It’s Finally Here, Thanks to the Aftermarket

Peitz Performance, which installed the TR9060 manual transaxle in the mid-engined ‘Vette, has a running and driving prototype at SEMA.

It was only a matter of time before someone successfully swapped a manual transmission into the C8 Corvette after Tremec revealed its TR9060 manual transaxle at the 2025 SEMA Show; indeed, the company even went so far as to say during last year’s show that it had already test-fit the transmission into a C8. And now, one year later, the swap we’ve been waiting for has become a reality.

Peitz Performance of Tomball, Texas is a well-known Corvette tuning shop, and they’re the first to have a running and driving C8-gen manual. It even has a listing on the company’s website with a price of $74,528.99 for the swap, and suggests the package will be available in July 2027. Exciting stuff, so let’s get into some of the details revealed at the 2026 SEMA Show.

The Tremec gearbox is operated via cable-controlled shifting. Peitz says the shifting mechanism is positioned on the left side of the transaxle housing. It also incorporates a concentric slave cylinder for clutch actuation.

Hot Rod had the chance to drive the C8 at SEMA, and along the way learned some more details about how Peitz made the swap come to life. One of the big advantages the tuner had going into the project is experience with the platform; most importantly, it already had 3D scans of the entire car. This made it easier to plan out how it would arrange everything in the tight confines of a mid-engine sports car.

The shifter itself started out life as a Porsche six-speed shifter, and a unique bracket was made to mount the clutch pedal to the brake pedal assembly. The pedal itself was taken from a CT4-V Blackwing, but modified with a pedal stop and hydraulic clutch assist. It needed a new flywheel, which includes the ring and teeth from a C8 flywheel but, of course, adds the clutch.

Making the new transmission play nice with all of the car’s electronics was one of the taller tasks, but it’s an area Peitz Performance is an expert in. Tuning DCT-equipped C8s and adding power to them is one of the shop’s specialties, so the team already understood the platform well.

The key is a Motec 182 Plug and Play with a Motec 150 for transmission control. With this, Peitz Performance can program in downshift throttle blips, upshift ignition cuts, and relay data like gear positions and transmission fluid temperature to a driver.

This package is still in development, and Peitz believes it will be in a final, installable form in the first quarter of 2027. The Tremec itself is good to support up to about 1000 pound-feet of torque and survive up to 8600 rpm. Its price of nearly $75,000 is mighty steep, but we suspect there will still be plenty of takers who would like a chance to row their own gears in the C8 Corvette.

#4528. DeepWay electric semi arrives in New Zealand, and gets a new name

New Zealand’s Foodstuffs North Island Limited has given its latest electric semi truck an electrifying new identity, courtesy of a second-grade student at a local elementary school.

The Chinese-built DeepWay Star began delivering chilled and frozen groceries across New Zealand’s lower North Island earlier this year – and, after a naming competition organized with students at Russell Street School in Palmerston North, the big HD EV has got a new name: Evie.

The winning name came from Year 2 (read: second grade) student named Madison, who beat out suggestions including Buzzy Bee, Lightning, and Bolt. Madison got to officially unveil the truck’s new name alongside her classmates, local officials and Foodstuffs representatives.

“Our trucks are out on the road every day delivering food to stores and communities, so we thought it would be great to get the kids involved and give our first electric truck a bit of personality,” explains Foodstuffs North Island General Manager Supply Chain, Yang Zhang. “There were some brilliant ideas, but Evie was a pretty fitting name for an EV. The best part is knowing Madison and the other students will be able to spot Evie out on the road and know they played a part in it.”

Madison was allowed to do the unveiling honors, revealing Evie’s new name alongside her other classmates, Palmerston North’s Mayor, Grant Smith, local MP Tangi Utikeri, and local PAK’nSAVE, New World, and Four Square grocers who will be receiving deliveries from Evie.

In its first few months on the road, Evie’s travelled nearly 45,000 kilometers (~28,000 miles) and avoided more than 81,000 kg of harmful carbon emissions – which the company claims is roughly equivalent to taking 35 ICE cars off the road for a full year.

As for the truck itself, it has a sort of Tesla-ish, anteater-y look, and significantly longer range than the StarWay, offering more than 500 km (~310 miles) of range from its 600 kWh CATL-built LFP battery packs that can plug into charge ports two at a time for lickety-quick charging in about 30 minutes. If that’s too long of a wait, the Star can swap its tired batteries for fresh ones in special battery-sway stations in just six minutes.

The DeepWay’s electric motors put out 491 kW (~660 hp) of power, and a positively tectonic 75,000 (!) Nm (~55,000 lb-ft) (!!) of torque – more than enough to get the 50 tons (100,000 lb.) of GVWR it’s rated for up to speed.

It is great to see electric trucks replacing Diesel. I just can’t understand why EV adoption is so slow to take off in New Zealand. It has plenty of great low cost EVs and petrol is all imported and expensive.

You can check out the pictures, above, then let us know what you think of the big Chinese BEV and it’s fun new name in the comments.

#4527. Electric cars are about to overtake petrol in the UK, data shows

Battery-electric cars took 32% of the UK’s new car market in October, while petrol cars fell to just 37.2%, according to new data from the SMMT. That’s the closest the two have been.

At the current pace, electric cars will outsell petrol in the UK within a year. And it could happen as soon as this December.

The UK registered 152,730 new cars in October, up 5.4% year-over-year and the 11th straight month of growth for the overall market.

All of that growth came from plug-ins. BEV registrations jumped 32.7% to 48,858 units, and plug-in hybrids rose 30.1% to 22,898. Meanwhile, petrol fell 11.6% to 56,876 units, diesel dropped 15.9%, and even conventional hybrids were down 5%.

Through the first 10 months of the year, the UK has now registered 503,805 BEVs, up 30.4%, for a 26.6% market share. Petrol’s year-to-date share is down to 41.1%, from 47.2% at the same point last year.

We pulled SMMT’s monthly fuel-type data going back to March 2024 to see where this is heading. Note that SMMT counts mild hybrids as petrol (or diesel) in its headline categories, and that’s generally how we count them at Electrek.

In March 2024, petrol held 55.9% of the market and BEVs 15.2%. In October 2026, it was 37.2% vs 32.0%. Petrol’s share is shrinking by about half a point per month on a linear trend, while BEVs gain about 0.36 points a month. Extend both lines and they cross around August 2027 at roughly 33% each.

But that’s the slow scenario, because it ignores December.

UK BEV share spikes every December as automakers push volume to get closer to their ZEV Mandate targets. BEVs hit 31.0% in December 2024 and 32.2% in December 2025, when petrol was at 39.4%. Over the last five months, BEV share has run about 5 points higher than a year earlier, and petrol about 7 points lower. If December follows that pattern, BEVs land around 37% and petrol around 32%.

That would be the first time BEVs beat petrol in SMMT’s headline numbers, mild hybrids included.

However, SMMT’s own forecast of 27.2% BEV share for the full year implies roughly 31% for November and December combined, which would make it a much closer call. And on a stricter definition that puts mild hybrids with hybrids instead of petrol, BEVs already outsold every other powertrain in August.

Zoom out to full years and the picture is just as clear. Cars that run only on petrol or diesel, mild hybrids included, made up 72.5% of the UK market in 2021. This year, they’re at 45.5%.

None of this is good enough for the SMMT, which is using the release to push the government, again, to cut the ZEV Mandate targets.

The mandate requires 33% of 2026 sales to be zero-emission. SMMT now forecasts 27.2%. It expects 32% next year against a 38% target, and 37.5% in 2028 against 52%, a 14.5-point gap.

The trade group says automakers have spent “billions” on discounts, 0% financing, deposit contributions, and even subsidized charging to move EVs, on top of the government’s Electric Car Grant. It also slammed last week’s Budget, which confirmed a new EV-specific road tax (eVED) starting in 2028 and kept 20% VAT on public charging.

“Higher targets may force supply, but they do not create demand,” SMMT chief executive Mike Hawes said.

We’ve heard this one before. The SMMT made the same argument after September’s record 99,199 BEV registrations, and the government already opened a review of the mandate this year.

This might be the main reason why the trade group wants to slow things down. The brands growing fastest in the UK are mostly Chinese. BYD registered 6,065 cars in October, up 73%. Jaecoo more than doubled to 6,089 units, Chery nearly tripled to 3,707, and Leapmotor doubled to 1,773. MG was up 85%.

Tesla, on the other hand, registered just 282 cars in October, down 45% from 511 a year ago. The first month of the quarter is always slow for Tesla in the UK, and the brand is still up 31% year-to-date at 46,526 units after a big September. But it didn’t have a single model in October’s top 10 BEVs, which was led by the Skoda Enyaq (1,568), Mini Countryman (1,494), and Jaecoo 5 (1,465).

The SMMT’s framing is that there’s a “demand gap.” The data shows the opposite. BEV registrations are up 30% this year while petrol is shrinking every single month. That’s not a market rejecting EVs.

The SMMT is not a neutral organisation, they have been briefing against EVs for years and continue to do so.

The ZEV mandate is NOT a measure of how many pure BEVs are sold, and the SMMT know it, it's a measure of REDUCING emission against a level set in the past.

Those emissions reductions can be met by selling BEVs, or selling more efficient PHEVs or even selling more efficient petrol or diesel cars! The manufacturers can also buy credits if they choose to.

NO manufacturer has paid any ZEV fines to date (DfT announcement March 2026)

As for the "heavy discounts" and "loss making sales", well I have two data points on that.

1. The retail price of EVs has continued to climb in the UK over the past 6 years, despite the cost of any average 50kWh battery pack dropping several thousand dollars.

2. There are hundreds of main dealerships who are buying cars from the manufacturers, driving them for the minimum 3 month period, often with just a few thousand miles on the clock and then selling them with a 30-35% retail price discount, and then repeating ad infinitum. The dealerships are still making a few thousand with each transaction, so we know where the manufacturers price really sits.

And the discounts automakers keep complaining about? That’s the mandate doing exactly what it was designed to do. It forces automakers to sell EVs, so they price them to sell, and buyers respond. Hawes says targets don’t create demand, but cheaper EVs clearly do. October proves it.

Now, is the jump to 52% in 2028 steep? It is steep, but it looks achievable to me. If anything is hurting demand, it’s the government’s own moves: a new EV-only road tax and 20% VAT on public charging. That’s what the industry should be fighting. It’s too early for that.

Either way, petrol’s days as the UK’s default car are numbered. The only question is whether the milestone comes in December or sometime in 2027. Our bet is December.

#4526. 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 Test: Capability, Comfort, and Style

With two new small-block V-8s, a new interior, and a wide-ranging trim lineup, the Silverado covers pickup needs from towing to dune jumps.

In ancient times, trucks were tools for farmers and construction workers. The idea that they should offer amenities like air conditioning or power steering would have been questionable, and the suggestion of heated seats or ambient lighting would have been laughed off the assembly line. We live in a gentler era, though, and the 2027 Chevy Silverado 1500 reflects the mainstream popularity of pickups for both work and play. Chevy’s half-ton lineup gets a major overhaul for the coming model year with reshaped sheetmetal; redesigned interiors featuring carbon fiber, wood, and bright pops of color; and two brand-new small-block V-8s that will delight internal-combustion loyalists.

Chevy has made enough changes to the Silverado for 2027 to call it a new generation, although what generation that is depends on if you’re starting your count from the first introduction of Silverado as its own model (1998) or all the way back to the first use of the name (1975, as a trim on the C/K models). We’re going from the ’90s, which would make this new truck the fifth generation. To earn its generational title, the Silverado wears a new exterior, crisp as a starched shirt, set off by LED lights, burly wheel lip moldings, and a redesigned bumper. Underneath, the chassis will be familiar from the previous year, albeit with some suspension tweaks for more stable towing and a better ride.

See all results for used cars for sale near 60629

The biggest news for truck fans won’t be the body styling or the interior decorating, but what’s under the big, angular hood. Lower trims still start out with an upgraded turbocharged 2.7-liter four-cylinder, now making 350 horsepower and 455 pound-feet of torque. Diesel fans get the returning Duramax turbo 3.0-liter inline-six, still rated at 305 horses and 495 pound-feet, but now with an optional 34-gallon fuel tank for a claimed (and bladder-challenging) 900-mile range.

And then there are the eight-cylinder stars of the show. These new V-8s are not bored-out versions of the outgoing 5.3- and 6.2-liter mills, but instead comprise completely new blocks, heads, intakes, and exhausts. The new engines measure out at 5.7 and 6.6 liters—or 346 and 401 cubic inches, for those speaking older tongues. Those designations were appealing enough to Chevrolet that they stamped them on the back of the aluminum blocks.

Most of our drive was divided between kitted-out High Country and rambunctious ZR2 models, both with the 6.6-liter, and we can report that the big small-block is powerful (481 ponies, 501 pound-feet), sonorous, and unexpectedly smooth, with elegant on-road manners and impressive trail performance. It’s also very quiet at idle, an effect of using newly added port fuel injection at low rpm and adding in direct injection as throttle input increases.

See all results for used cars for sale near 60629

Back at the C/D homestead, we spent time with the 402-hp, 428-lb-ft 5.7-liter V-8 in the lesser off-road-oriented Trail Boss trim. The Trail Boss is the light-beer equivalent of the hoppy ZR2, offering some trail tech without going all-in on off-road. A roughly two-inch suspension lift, 34-inch Goodyear Wrangler Territory MT tires on 18-inch wheels, and optional underbody cameras give the Trail Boss gravel-road cred. On the pavement, the Trail Boss rides with a little more rear-end jiggle than the High Country (with its adaptive dampers) or the ZR2 (with its Multimatic DSSV setup). At the test track, the Boss got to 60 mph in a reasonable 6.4 seconds and covered the quarter-mile in 14.6 seconds at its 94-mph top speed. But its dirt-focused rubber likely hampered its performance elsewhere. Braking from 70 mph took 198 feet and a twirl around the skidpad returned just 0.70 g of grip while fighting some unsurprising understeer.

In the real world, the Trail Boss felt quicker and more planted than its test results suggest, and the 5.7 offers nearly silent running (a mere 66 decibels and 21 sones at 70 mph). It’d better, given its $2690 option price. When combined with other options on our test truck, covering everything from multi-camera arrays to a slick coat of green paint, our mid-price model ended up with an as-tested window sticker of $76,795. That much scratch could get you into a rear-wheel-drive High Country model with the 5.7 or within spitting distance of a Duramax-equipped ZR2. Upgrading either of those trims to the 6.6-liter (not available on the Trail Boss) would require an extra $2505 for the ZR2 and $2800 for the High Country, with the latter also mandating an upgrade to 4WD. These new V-8s are slick but dear.

Even the base 2.7-liter work truck has a starting price of $40,045, but at least the lower trims benefit from some of the same features as the top-shelf models. The Silverado’s interior rework means that every 2027 truck showcases data on a 12.2-inch gauge cluster and a 16.3-inch center screen. ZR2 and High Country trims get an additional 11.5-inch passenger screen. The displays mark the return of Android Auto and Apple Car Play, but the system still includes Google built-in nav and search functions. We found the native navigation prone to directional confusion, so we’re glad GM walked back its plans to ditch phone mirroring.

The new GM UI is crisp and quick, but we had some issues with the touchscreen’s accuracy. Organizationally, the Silverado interior is scattered, with some controls on the left side of the dash, some in menus in the touchscreen, and some on hard buttons above the console. Chevy allows for menu customizations that create shortcuts to regularly used controls, but until a customer sets that up, they should be prepared for a hunt.

Dialing in the least-irritating combination of driver assist functions might take some time, but setting up for a proper truck job like towing will not. And it’ll handle a proper truck job: The new light-duty Chevy now boasts up to 13,700 pounds of max towing capacity (when properly equipped). The Silverado offers helpful setup and safety tech like a trailer brake-gain assistant for setting trailer brake proportions, as well as several split-view camera angles with overlay graphics that promise to make parking easier and prevent a jackknife. Super Cruise–equipped trucks can tow with the system running, although automatic lane changes are not available while towing.

The Silverado lineup includes everything from a regular cab with an extended cargo bed to the feature-heavy crew-cab top trims. The cabin is noticeably nicer than previous models, and the crew cab will comfortably fit a large, er, crew. Pickup trucks have changed a lot in the past century—largely for the better—but with increased comfort and capability come increased prices. No matter how good the Silverado’s two new V-8s are, there’s no way to drive around that truth.

#4525. Alan Jones, 1980 Formula 1 World Champion, Has Died

The Australian world champion was 80 years old.

Alan Jones, an Australian racing icon and the 1980 Formula 1 world champion, has died after a brief illness. He had just turned 80 years old.

Jones took a long route from Australia to Formula 1, moving to Europe first in 1967 and working through a variety of odd series before debuting in a privately-owned Hesketh in 1975. He then ran in stints for Graham Hill and John Surtees before joining Shadow, one of the strangest teams in F1 history. He would win the 1977 Austrian Grand Prix for the team, his first victory and what would be the only win the team ever claimed in F1. Jones finished the season in seventh, and suddenly became a major player in the series.

In 1978, he joined a recently re-formed Williams Grand Prix Engineering. This was the second F1 team run by Frank Williams, one that was not yet a powerhouse. Williams became a force to be reckoned with quickly after Jones joined, allowing the Australian driver to establish himself as a player in F1 with four wins in the 1979 season. That number ballooned to five in 1980, earning him the title by 13 points over future Williams champion Nelson Piquet. He also guided the team to its first constructor’s title.

Jones missed out on the 1981 driver’s title, but he and teammate Carlos Reutemann guided the Williams operation to its second of what has since become nine constructor’s championships. He retired after that year, although he would occasionally show up on the grid in parts of three more seasons.

In the decades that followed, Jones became a mainstay in the Australian touring car championship that evolved into what we now know as Supercars. He won five races in a career that stretched until 2002, entering the Bathurst 1000 19 times. Jones never won that race, nor did he win the 24 Hours of Le Mans in his two starts in that event, but he remained a presence in auto racing for decades.

Australia’s Nine reports that Jones received a cancer diagnosis “only weeks ago.” He is survived by his wife and four children.
